options.summary: Permissive, minimal, the most common choice for small tools and skills.
consequences: Anyone may use, copy, modify, merge, publish, distribute, sublicense and sell, provided the copyright and licence notice are retained.
No patent grant and no express trademark grant.
Consistent with the existing MIT declaration on skills/sps-cms.
Anyone may privately fork and close-source their derivative.

options.summary: Permissive, with an explicit patent grant and a patent-retaliation clause.
consequences: The same broad permissions as MIT, plus an express patent licence from contributors.
Requires NOTICE-preserving change-log discipline on redistribution.
Expressly terminates the patent grant for patent-initiating litigation.
Compatible with MIT-licensed sps-cms, but the NOTICE obligation is stricter.

options.summary: Permissive; like MIT plus a no-endorsement clause.
consequences: Bars use of contributor names to promote derived products.
Otherwise similar to MIT, with no patent grant.
Modified MPL-covered files must remain MPL and be published when distributed.
Larger files may be combined with proprietary code without the copyleft spreading.
Higher ongoing compliance burden than a fully permissive licence.
Any distributed derivative must be GPL-3.0 and its source published.
Viral for combined works and incompatible with some proprietary redistribution.
Unsuitable if SPS is intended to stay closed-source or to allow closed forks.

options.summary: Strong copyleft extending to network use.
consequences: Also requires source publication when the software is offered over a network.
The strictest option listed; usually unsuitable for internal tooling.

options.summary: Keep today's default: ship no licence file at all.
consequences: This is the legal default now and is itself a valid, deliberate choice.
Gate D continues to block promotion; the P4 outcome does not change.
No one may legally copy, modify or redistribute the work.
Permissive reuse is impossible, which may be the intent for a personal toolset.
